title: The first sermon, alone
tomorrow: the teacher is dying. what does he leave them with?

cards: Some weeks the advice online swings between two camps. Treat yourself, you deserve it. Or: discipline everything, no excuses, cold showers forever.
Either way you're promised it'll finally fix you. SN 56.11 opens on a similar fork. In the Deer Park near Benares, the Buddha speaks to a group of five monks, old companions in hard practice.
His first words to them are about two roads not to take.

teach.b: Read it alone and it's short and plain. In paraphrase: there are two extremes. One is chasing pleasure, low and leading nowhere.
The other is punishing yourself, painful and leading nowhere. Avoiding both, there's a middle way that brings vision and peace: the noble eightfold path. Then the four truths, laid down like stones.

There is suffering: birth, aging, sickness, death, being stuck with what you don't want, separated from what you love, not getting what you wish for. It has a cause: craving, the thirst that keeps reaching.
It can end, when that craving fades and is let go.

teach.h: SUFFERING, ITS CAUSE, ITS END, A PATH.
teach.b: And there's a path to that end, the same eightfold path. Notice where the list of suffering lands. Not only death and sickness.

teach.h: NOT GETTING WHAT YOU WISH FOR.
teach.b: Not getting what you wish for. A mother who can't give the easy yes. A daughter who can't hear it.
Then one of the five, Kondanna, understands: whatever arises also ceases.
And, the sutta says, the cry goes up that the wheel of the teaching has been set rolling. Nobody can turn it back.

how: The first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, is chanted in Theravada communities, and Asalha Puja, a full-moon holy day, remembers its teaching.

o: a prayer monks recite before their first meal
the sutta where the wheel of the teaching was set rolling
the Buddha's speech at his own father's palace

games.q: inside the first sermon — tap the pairs.

s: the middle way means doing everything in moderation
it's a path between two extremes, chasing pleasure and punishing yourself: the eightfold path.
the sutta's list of suffering includes not getting what you wish for
beside birth, aging, sickness and death.
the first truth says life is only suffering
it says there is suffering, then that it has a cause, can end, and has a path.

games.q: you blew your savings on a trip and now want to ban yourself from spending anything for a year. what does the first sermon say?
o: neither binge nor punishment: find the middle way between them
the ban is right; strictness is the cure for indulgence
you've already slipped, so you might as well keep spending
games.why: the sermon opens by naming both extremes, chasing pleasure and punishing yourself, as leading nowhere. the path runs between them.

practice: Say the four truths from memory, quietly, in your own short words: there is suffering; it has a cause; it can end; there's a path. Say them once more, slower. Then sit, and let the words settle like the stones they are.

wordCard.voice: The first sermon: SN 56.11, the setting in motion of the wheel. Two extremes, a middle way, four truths.

orig.note: Pali: the wheel (cakka) of the teaching (dhamma). The sutta is the setting in motion of it.

carryVoice: Your line: the wheel. Once it's rolling, nobody can turn it back. Sutta four, read alone.
